statements.quote: This chapter has two halves.
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: The first asks a question that took two thousand years to be *asked*: **what makes a procedure an *algorithm*?** — and follows the answer through Euclid's gcd, the Sieve of Eratosthenes, and the 1928 decision problem that forced the entire theory of computation to be invented.
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: The second shows a modern transformer *executing* algorithms on its own: grokking the Discrete Fourier Transform without being told it, and running code that exists only in the prompt.
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: Read the first half to understand the object being executed; the second is the machine that runs it.
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: You have used the word *algorithm* so many times it has lost all meaning.
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: A sorting step is an algorithm.
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: A search is an algorithm.
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: The way your coffee machine cycles through its modes is, in the strict sense, an algorithm.
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: But there is a question almost nobody asks, and it is the one this whole field was eventually built around: **what makes a procedure an *algorithm* — as opposed to just a set of steps you happen to run?**
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: Two properties, and they are the entire game.
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: * **It must terminate.** An algorithm is not an infinite loop.
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: It must *finish*, in a finite number of steps, for every input it promises to handle.
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: * **It must be correct — by construction.** Not "it usually works," not "we tested a few cases," but *guaranteed* right, by an argument that holds for *every* input.
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: A procedure that has both is an algorithm.
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: The rest of this half is the story of those two properties — and of how, in a single decade, they went from being quietly *practiced* for two thousand years to being rigorously *studied*.
statements.section: Two Lessons in One

statements.quote: One of the oldest algorithms still in use every day sits in Euclid's *Elements*, Book VII (\cite[Euclidean algorithm]{euclideanalgorithm}; \cite[The Elements]{euclidelements}); Babylonian scribes were already writing step-by-step procedures a millennium and a half earlier (\cite[Knuth, 1972]{knuth1972babylonian}).
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: Given two whole numbers, find their **greatest common divisor** — the largest number that divides both.
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: > Divide the larger by the smaller.
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: Replace the pair by *(the smaller, the remainder)*.
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: Repeat until the remainder is zero.
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: The last non-zero remainder is the answer.
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: It is an algorithm in the full, strong sense — and the *why* is the point, because it is the earliest example we have of someone *checking the two properties*.
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: * **Termination.** Each remainder is smaller than the divisor it came from, and a remainder is always smaller than the divisor.
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: So the second number of the pair, the divisor, strictly shrinks at every step.
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: A list of positive integers that keeps shrinking cannot go on forever — it *must* reach zero.
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: That is not a hope that it will stop; it is a proof that it will.
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: * **Correctness.** The load-bearing fact is $gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a - qb)$: taking away a multiple of one number from the other never changes the two numbers' common divisor.
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: Every single step preserves the answer; and when the process ends, the answer is sitting in the last non-zero remainder.
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: For the next two thousand years, this was just *the way you found a common divisor*.
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: Nobody wrote "this procedure provably terminates and is provably correct," because the idea of checking those two things **in general** had not yet occurred to anyone.
statements.section: Euclid's algorithm (c. 300 BC): the first with a surviving proof

statements.quote: A few decades later, in Alexandria, the same two millennia-old craft produced a different *shape* of procedure: the \cite[Sieve of Eratosthenes]{sieveoferatosthenes}.
statements.section: Another shape of algorithm: the Sieve of Eratosthenes (c. 240 BC)

statements.quote: Given a limit $n$, list every number from 2 to $n$, then cross off every multiple of 2, then every multiple of 3, then 5, and so on.
statements.section: Another shape of algorithm: the Sieve of Eratosthenes (c. 240 BC)

statements.quote: What is left standing is exactly the set of primes.
statements.section: Another shape of algorithm: the Sieve of Eratosthenes (c. 240 BC)

statements.quote: Where Euclid's algorithm *reduces* a problem step by step, the sieve **filters** a finite set.
statements.section: Another shape of algorithm: the Sieve of Eratosthenes (c. 240 BC)

statements.quote: It is still an algorithm, for the same two reasons: it *terminates* (once the smallest number you have not crossed off, $p$, satisfies $p^2 > n$, nothing below $n$ can still be composite, so you are done), and it is *correct by construction* (a number survives the sieve only if none of the primes below it divide it, which is precisely what being prime means).
statements.section: Another shape of algorithm: the Sieve of Eratosthenes (c. 240 BC)

statements.quote: Two algorithms, separated by a few decades and a city, both defined long before the word *computer* existed, both pinned down by the identical pair: **it stops, and it is right.**
statements.section: Another shape of algorithm: the Sieve of Eratosthenes (c. 240 BC)

statements.quote: Here is the gap the rest of the course has been circling.
statements.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

statements.quote: For all that, the algorithm was never a **thing**.
statements.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

statements.quote: People *did* algorithms; no one *studied* them as objects with properties you could check.
statements.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

statements.quote: The name is itself a fossil of that gap.
statements.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

statements.quote: *Algorithm* is the Latinized form of the name of the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi, whose ninth-century arithmetic gave us the word \cite[the etymology of "algorithm" (Wikipedia)]{historyofmath_wikipedia} — the course traces al-Khwarizmi himself in [The Brief History of AI](history.php).
statements.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

statements.quote: But al-Khwarizmi *named and catalogued* procedures — he did not ask the question that actually matters, and that nobody had asked before:
statements.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

statements.quote: > Is there a **general, universal** procedure?
statements.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

statements.quote: Can one machine, running one rule, decide the answer to *any* problem in a class — not just *this* gcd, or *this* sieve, but *any* instance, for all time?
statements.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

statements.quote: Naming a class of things is not the same as asking whether the class has a single procedure that handles all of it.
statements.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

statements.quote: That question — and it is *the* question — sat unasked until the twentieth century.
statements.section: The gap: two thousand years of *doing*, none of *studying*

statements.quote: 820) is the bridge between the Babylonian recipe and the modern algorithm: it states a general procedure for solving quadratics and then demonstrates it on every case, with a geometric proof for each.

statements.quote: Two very different algorithms mark the long middle.
statements.section: The long middle: from method to program

statements.quote: Newton's method, circulated in the 1670s and published in his *Method of Fluxions*, finds a root by repeatedly replacing a guess $x$ with $x - f(x)/f'(x)$; its convergence can be proved, and its descendants still solve equations inside every numerical library (\cite[Newton, 1736]{newton1736fluxions}).
statements.section: The long middle: from method to program

statements.quote: In 1843 Ada Lovelace published a step-by-step program for Babbage's Analytical Engine to compute Bernoulli numbers -- the first published program for a general-purpose machine -- and argued that such a machine could manipulate symbols, not only numbers (\cite[Menabrea & Lovelace, 1843]{menabrea_lovelace1843}; \cite[Ada Lovelace]{ada_lovelace_wiki}).
statements.section: The long middle: from method to program

statements.quote: In 1928 the mathematician David Hilbert (\cite[Hilbert & Ackermann, 1928]{hilbert1928entscheidung}) posed a question that had been waiting, unasked, for two thousand years.
statements.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

statements.quote: In German it is the **Entscheidungsproblem**, the decision problem:
statements.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

statements.quote: > Given any statement of arithmetic — or, more generally, any formula of logic — does there exist a **general, mechanical procedure** that decides, in a finite number of steps, whether the statement is provable?
statements.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

statements.quote: This is exactly the question Euclid's two properties had been pointing at all along.
statements.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

statements.quote: An *algorithm* was, quietly, a candidate *answer*: a mechanical procedure that terminates and is correct.
statements.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

statements.quote: The Entscheidungsproblem asks whether such a procedure exists **in general** — not for this problem, but for the whole class.
statements.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

statements.quote: Hilbert was confident the answer was **yes**; he was actively looking for the procedure.
statements.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

statements.quote: The answer, delivered eight years later by two independent mathematicians wielding two tools that looked nothing alike, was **no**.
statements.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

statements.quote: \marginfig{hilbert_1907.jpg}{David Hilbert (1862–1943), 1907.
statements.section: The question that built everything: the Entscheidungsproblem (1928)

statements.quote: Kurt Gödel had already delivered the first blow in 1931 with his incompleteness theorems \cite[Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931)]{godel1931incompleteness}: no consistent, effectively axiomatized system that can express basic arithmetic can prove every true statement in it.
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: But incompleteness left a door open — it says some truths escape *proof*, not that no *procedure* could still decide which statements are decidable.
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: The decision problem was still, as far as anyone could tell, on the table.
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: In 1936, working independently, **Alonzo Church** and **Alan Turing** each wrote down a rigorous formalism for "mechanical procedure," and each used it to answer the 1928 question with a proof that the answer is **no** \cite[The Church–Turing Thesis (SEP)]{churchturing1936}.
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: Turing learned of Church's result while his own paper was in press, and added an appendix proving the two formalisms equivalent.
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: * **Church** worked with the λ-calculus: pure rewriting of symbols, a formalism that reads like algebra.
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: * **Turing** built a *machine* — a finite controller that reads one symbol at a time from, and writes symbols to, an infinite strip of tape, moving left or right according to its current state \cite[Turing, On Computable Numbers (1936)]{turing1937}.
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: The two formalisms look nothing alike.
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: One is a calculus; the other is a physical picture of a head on a tape.
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: And yet they compute *exactly* the same set of functions — every problem one can solve, the other can solve too.
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: That coincidence is so load-bearing that it has its own name: the \cite[Church–Turing thesis (SEP)]{churchturing1936}.
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: And the upshot for the 1928 question: within this shared class of "what a machine can do," the validity of a first-order formula is not decidable in general.
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: The Entscheidungsproblem has *no solution* — not because no one was clever enough to find the procedure, but because the procedure is provably *not there*.
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: The question itself has no "yes."
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: A Turing machine: a finite set of states reading and writing symbols on an infinite tape, moving left or right.
statements.section: 1936: two machines, one answer

statements.quote: Step back, and the whole chapter is one turning point.
statements.section: The payoff: the algorithm becomes an object

statements.quote: * For two millennia, people **ran** procedures — Euclid's gcd, the sieve — and never asked *what made them work*.
statements.section: The payoff: the algorithm becomes an object

statements.quote: * One question — *is there a general method?* (the Entscheidungsproblem, 1928) — forced the procedure itself to become a **mathematical object** with checkable properties: *does it terminate?
statements.section: The payoff: the algorithm becomes an object

statements.quote: what is it even able to reach?*
statements.section: The payoff: the algorithm becomes an object

statements.quote: * Answering that question (Church, Turing, 1936) did not merely settle a logic puzzle.
statements.section: The payoff: the algorithm becomes an object

statements.quote: It **invented the theory of computation** — the study of *computation as a thing you can reason about*, not just a thing you do.
statements.section: The payoff: the algorithm becomes an object

statements.quote: That is the "displaced prerequisite" this first half is filling.
statements.section: The payoff: the algorithm becomes an object

statements.quote: Everything in the second half of this chapter, and in [Software](software.php) — the idea that a computation has a *cost*, a *guarantee*, and a *limit* — rests on the fact that, in 1936, the algorithm stopped being a verb and became a noun.
statements.section: The payoff: the algorithm becomes an object

statements.quote: You can now hold one in your hand and take it apart: ask whether it stops, prove whether it is right, and measure how much work it does.
statements.section: The payoff: the algorithm becomes an object

statements.quote: Euclid had the algorithm.

statements.quote: Hilbert asked the question.
statements.section: The payoff: the algorithm becomes an object

statements.quote: Church and Turing built the machine that *is* the answer.

statements.quote: > A procedure becomes an **algorithm** when two things hold: it **terminates** for every input it promises to handle, and it is **correct by construction**.
statements.section: The payoff: the algorithm becomes an object

statements.quote: The question "is there a *general* procedure?" — the Entscheidungsproblem, 1928 — is what turned that property from a verb into an object, and forced the entire theory of computation to be built.

statements.quote: The mid-twentieth century made algorithms into engineering objects.
statements.section: What an algorithm costs

statements.quote: Binary search -- repeatedly halving a sorted interval -- was described by John Mauchly in 1946 and analyzed in the early 1960s; Knuth's *Sorting and Searching* gave its exact comparison count and a canonical correct formulation (\cite[Binary search]{binarysearch_wiki}; \cite[Knuth]{taocp3}).
statements.section: What an algorithm costs

statements.quote: Dijkstra's 1968 letter against the `goto` statement argued that programs should be built from structured control flow so their progress can be reasoned about, and Hoare's 1969 axioms gave a formal logic for assignments and while-loops -- the beginning of program verification (\cite[Dijkstra, 1968]{dijkstra1968goto}; \cite[Hoare, 1969]{hoare1969axiomatic}).
statements.section: What an algorithm costs

statements.quote: Two questions turned algorithms into a mathematical theory.
statements.section: What an algorithm costs

statements.quote: Cook (1971) and Levin (1973) showed that a single problem -- Boolean satisfiability -- is complete for the class NP: if it had a polynomial-time algorithm, so would every problem whose solution can be checked in polynomial time (\cite[Cook, 1971]{cook1971complexity}; \cite[Cook-Levin theorem]{cooklevin_wiki}).
statements.section: What an algorithm costs

statements.quote: Bellman's *Dynamic Programming* (1957) gave the complementary positive technique: break a problem into overlapping subproblems, store each answer once, and build the optimum from optimal subproblems (\cite[Bellman, 1957]{bellman1957book}).
statements.section: What an algorithm costs

statements.quote: Together they defined the modern question -- not just can it be computed, but at what cost.
statements.section: What an algorithm costs

statements.quote: Two algorithms from the same decades made whole industries computable.
statements.section: What an algorithm costs

statements.quote: Dantzig's simplex method (1947; book 1963) solved linear programs by walking along the vertices of a polyhedron, turning logistics, scheduling, and resource allocation into routine calculation (\cite[Dantzig, 1963]{dantzig1963linear}).
statements.section: What an algorithm costs

statements.quote: The fast Fourier transform, rediscovered by Cooley and Tukey in 1965, reduced the cost of a discrete Fourier transform from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n\log n)$; Gauss had used the same idea in 1805, but the 1965 paper made it a standard tool (\cite[Cooley & Tukey, 1965]{cooley1965fft}; \cite[FFT history]{fft_history_wiki}).
statements.section: What an algorithm costs

statements.quote: Modern algorithms increasingly search rather than calculate.
statements.section: What an algorithm costs

statements.quote: PageRank (1998) treated the web as a Markov chain and ranked pages by the stationary distribution of a random surfer, turning a graph into a single global importance score (\cite[Brin & Page, 1998]{brin1998pagerank}).
statements.section: What an algorithm costs

statements.quote: AlphaGo (2016) combined a policy network, a value network, and Monte Carlo tree search to beat Lee Sedol at Go -- a game whose branching factor had defeated pure search (\cite[Silver et al., 2016]{silver2016go}).
statements.section: What an algorithm costs

statements.quote: Both are algorithms in the old sense -- they terminate and are correct relative to a model -- but their guarantee is statistical or empirical, not a proof of optimality.
statements.section: What an algorithm costs

statements.quote: The concept is settled: an algorithm is a procedure that terminates and is correct, and since 1936 we can *reason* about algorithms — their cost, their guarantees, their limits.
statements.section: How a Transformer Executes Algorithms

statements.quote: The second half of this chapter asks a concrete question: can a *neural network* actually *run* one?
statements.section: How a Transformer Executes Algorithms

statements.quote: A transformer trained on a toy arithmetic task does two things that look almost impossible.
statements.section: How a Transformer Executes Algorithms

statements.quote: It **groks** an algorithm it was never explicitly taught — it rediscovers the Discrete Fourier Transform on its own.
statements.section: How a Transformer Executes Algorithms

statements.quote: And it **executes code that only exists in the prompt** — an algorithm it has never seen before, following it step by step with no interpreter and no CPU.
statements.section: How a Transformer Executes Algorithms

statements.quote: Both are real, measured, and explained below, starting with how a tiny network computes modular addition by rotating points on a circle.
statements.section: How a Transformer Executes Algorithms

statements.quote: When we train a neural network on a simple task like modular addition, something remarkable happens.
statements.section: How a Transformer Executes Algorithms

statements.quote: The network doesn't just memorize the answers, it *discovers* an algorithm.
statements.section: How a Transformer Executes Algorithms

statements.quote: Specifically, it learns to use the **Discrete Fourier Transform** to convert addition into wave interference, as described by (\cite[Nanda et al., 2023]{nanda2023grokking}).
statements.section: How a Transformer Executes Algorithms

statements.quote: This section walks through, step by step, exactly *how* a tiny one-layer Transformer computes:
statements.section: How a Transformer Executes Algorithms

statements.quote: where $P = 113$ is a prime number.
statements.section: How a Transformer Executes Algorithms

statements.quote: The network's vocabulary is just the numbers $\{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 112\}$, and it must output the correct sum modulo 113.
statements.section: How a Transformer Executes Algorithms

statements.quote: The network learns that **modular arithmetic is circular**.
statements.section: The Core Insight

statements.quote: After $P$, you wrap around to 0, just like an angle wrapping around a circle.
statements.section: The Core Insight

statements.quote: So the network represents each number as a **point on a circle**, and performs addition by **rotating angles**.
statements.section: The Core Insight

statements.quote: But a single circle (a single frequency) has too many ambiguities.
statements.section: The Core Insight

statements.quote: So the network uses **5 different frequencies** simultaneously, and combines them via **constructive interference**, the same principle that makes noise-cancelling headphones work, but in reverse.
statements.section: The Core Insight

statements.quote: The trained network implements the following algorithm (\cite[Nanda et al., 2023, Section 4]{nanda2023grokking}):
statements.section: The Algorithm in Five Steps

statements.quote: **Embedding:** Map each input number to points on 5 different circles (5 Fourier components)
statements.section: The Algorithm in Five Steps

statements.quote: **Attention:** Bring the representations of $a$ and $b$ together
statements.section: The Algorithm in Five Steps

statements.quote: **MLP:** Apply trigonometric addition theorems to compute $\cos(\omega_k(a+b))$ and $\sin(\omega_k(a+b))$
statements.section: The Algorithm in Five Steps

statements.quote: **Unembedding:** Compare the result against all 113 possible output tokens using cosine similarity

statements.quote: The circular representations above solve a very specific problem: **modular** addition, where the answer wraps around a fixed modulus ($\bmod N$).
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: That is a *bounded, cyclic* task — there is no "carry out to infinity," and no question of how *big* a number is.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: Once you leave that world, the model hits two different walls, and understanding them clarifies what a "number" actually is inside the network.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: **Magnitude, not value.** The natural question is how the model represents *size* — how does it "know" that $7 > 3$ so it can compare two numbers?
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: (\cite[Levy & Geva, 2024]{levy2024numbers}) probed and intervened on Llama-3-8B and Mistral-7B and found that they do **not** store a single ordered "number line." Instead **each digit is stored as its own circular (angular) code in base 10**: the value of a digit $d$ sits at the angle $\theta = 2\pi d / 10$ around a small circle, held in a *pair* of dimensions as $(\cos\theta,\; \sin\theta)$.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: So a digit is a 2-D rotary code — the same kind of Fourier feature the modular-addition section used, just applied one digit at a time.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: Crucially, each *digit position* (units, tens, hundreds, …) gets its **own separate** circle in its own (roughly orthogonal) 2-D subspace, so the digits do not bleed into each other.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: "13" is therefore not a point between 12 and 14 — it is a "1" on the *tens* circle plus a "3" on the *units* circle.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: In the **hidden states (the residual stream) of the later layers**, not in the input embedding.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: The circular probes decode the digits reliably from about the **third layer onward** (the first couple of layers are still busy "contextualizing" a multi-digit number, whose several tokens have to be combined first), and a causal intervention that rotates one digit's angle by $+5 \bmod 10$ modifies that digit in the model's answer — the exact intended result appears in only about 10–15% of cases (roughly half are "close"), so the code is genuinely *used*, not merely readable.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: (The paper's honest caveat: this is one strong, causally-active representation; it may be one of several redundant ones packed in superposition, not the only numeracy signal.) The tell-tale signature is the *error pattern*: arithmetic mistakes cluster on a **single digit** of the answer (the model emits "633" or "823" instead of "833"), exactly what a digit-wise code predicts — not the value-adjacent slips ("831", "834") a real number-line representation would produce.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: There is no clean, monotonic magnitude to "read off" and compare, which is why comparing small numbers is so error-prone: the model holds a digit-by-digit code, not a quantity.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: \cite[Cacioli (2026)]{cacioli2026weber} brought the formal tools of psychophysics to the question.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: First, **Weber's law** — a 19th-century finding about human perception: the smallest difference you can notice between two stimuli is a constant *fraction* of their size, not a constant *amount*.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: You tell 10 from 11 instantly, but not 1000 from 1001, because the gap (1) shrinks relative to the magnitude.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: The consequence is that magnitudes are spaced **logarithmically** in perception: a fixed *ratio* (×1.1) is a fixed *distance*, whether you are near 10 or near 1000.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: (\cite[Cacioli, 2026]{cacioli2026weber}) found the transformer's magnitude geometry has exactly this **log-compressive, Weber-law** structure (a 10% step is a constant distance), which also resolves a live disagreement in the literature (linear spacing?
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: But the decisive finding is a **dissociation**: a model can *have* this logarithmic magnitude geometry and *still* perform at chance on discrimination tasks.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: Representing magnitude and being *able to use it to compare* are not the same thing — the geometry is necessary but not sufficient.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: **Counting: recognizing is not counting.** "How many r's are in strawberry?" is the canonical failing.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: (\cite[Fu et al., 2024]{fu2024count}) showed that models **recognize the letters but do not count them**: errors track the number of letters/tokens in the word, and the dominant failure is that *most models break once a symbol repeats more than twice*.
statements.section: Beyond Modular Arithmetic: Magnitude, Comparison, and Counting

statements.quote: Word frequency in the training data barely matters — this is a computation they are performing on the fly, not a lookup they failed to memorize.

statements.quote: (\cite[Conde et al., 2025]{conde2025count}) confirmed exact counting is not intrinsic; it only becomes reliable when the model is given a scratchpad (a chain-of-thought it can increment).

statements.quote: **Why it is hard, in principle.** The difference from modular addition is not training data — it is the *shape of the state required*.

statements.quote: Mod-$N$ addition lives on a finite circle, so it needs only a bounded, cyclic representation (exactly the Fourier features above \cite[Ding et al., 2024]{ding2024fittest} \cite[Engels et al., 2025]{engels2024multidim}).

statements.quote: Exact counting, by contrast, needs an **unbounded integer** that increments and is read out at the end — a state that grows with the input.

statements.quote: \cite[Hahn (2020)]{hahn2020limitations} proved the matching impossibility: a fixed-size transformer's self-attention **cannot model periodic finite-state languages** (counting to $n$, parity, "how many times does $x$ appear") **unless the number of layers or heads grows with the sequence length.** In other words, a fixed network has no reliable exact-integer counter, and the depth that would supply one is exactly what is fixed.

statements.quote: An RNN keeps its state in a single hidden vector that it updates one token at a time, carrying everything forward.

statements.quote: A transformer has **no such carried-over hidden vector**: within a single forward pass it is a *parallel* function applied to the whole context at once, with no step-by-step evolution.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: You are right that "time" barely exists for the network inside one forward pass — the only real notion of order is the **sequence position** of the tokens (and, during generation, the autoregressive step-by-step decoding).
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: So "state across time" below means **state across the token positions / decode steps**, not an internal clock.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: Given that, the puzzle is sharper, not softer: how can a network with no carried-over memory do anything *sequential* or *stateful* — parse a sentence, follow a procedure, track a running count — when it has nowhere to keep the running total?
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: The reframe is that the state is **not absent, it is distributed**.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: The "state" is the **residual stream plus the Key/Value vectors of every past token**.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: Each past token's hidden state is a register that the current token can read from through attention, and each new token writes a fresh entry.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: The whole sequence is, in effect, a **work tape / register file** that the model re-reads every step.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: (\cite[Katharopoulos et al., 2020]{katharopoulos2020linear}) made the relationship to recurrence literal: a *linear*-attention transformer has an exact **iterative (RNN-like) implementation**, where a single accumulated matrix plays the role of the hidden state.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: "Stateless" is therefore a misnomer; the state is just stored *in the context* rather than in a vector.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: Formally, this is enough to run a state machine.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: A single attention layer can implement the transitions of a **finite-state automaton** — softly, through the softmax, or exactly under a hardmax.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: (\cite[Adriaensen & Maene, 2024]{adriaensen2024moore}) took this concretely: they trained transformers on regular languages and then **extracted the finite-state (Moore) machine the network had implicitly built**, using queries and counterexamples rather than reading the states out of the weights.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: You can pull the state machine *out* of the transformer.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: But the power is bounded, and (\cite[Hahn, 2020]{hahn2020limitations}) pins down where.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: Because the context length is fixed, the number of distinct "states" a single forward pass can hold is finite — a fixed-size, fixed-context transformer is a **finite-state machine**, and it cannot model periodic or truly hierarchical languages unless its depth or head-count scales with the input.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: The mechanistic engine behind the sequential behavior is the **induction head** (\cite[Olsson et al., 2022]{olsson2022induction}) — find $[A][B]\ldots[A]$, copy the successor $[B]$ — which is a primitive form of **recurrence** (copy what followed a repeated pattern).
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: And (\cite[von Oswald et al., 2022]{vonoswald2022indc}) read the whole forward pass as **in-context gradient descent**, with the residual stream holding an *evolving in-context model*.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: So "recurrence" in a transformer is not a stored hidden vector being updated; it is attention **re-reading an ever-growing store of past states** and refining them layer by layer, a hand-off between specialized heads in successive layers that is carried by thin low-rank "channels" in the residual stream (\cite[Merullo et al., 2024]{merullo2024talkingheads}).
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: The honest summary: a transformer performs sequential, stateful computation by treating the context itself as state — a soft state machine whose state space is bounded by its (fixed) depth and context window.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State

statements.quote: That bound is precisely what limits the arithmetic and counting of the previous section, and the binding limits you meet in the fact-retrieval chapter.
statements.section: A Transformer as a State Machine: How a Stateless Network Keeps State
